co_frisky_cliff.blurb: Frisky Cliff is a compact crag high in Boulder Canyon, around 8,000 feet, with fifteen routes of roughly 40 to 100 feet. Twelve are bolted sport lines and three are gear routes. The climbing is steep and hard: more than half the routes fall in the 5.13 range, with a handful of 5.12s, a few 5.10 and 5.11 lines, and a single 5.8 as the easy outlier. It is a destination for strong sport climbers rather than beginners. The wall holds shade through the morning and early afternoon, which helps on warm days, and it sees fewer visitors than the canyon's roadside cliffs.

co_cenotaph_crag.blurb: Cenotaph Crag is a small, quiet cliff on the north side of Boulder Canyon at about 8,000 feet. Most of the fifteen routes are traditional lines of 35 to 50 feet, with a couple of bolted sport routes, a top-rope problem and one hard boulder problem. Grades cluster between 5.9 and 5.11, and there are a couple of easier lines in the 5.7 and 5.8 range. The rock is blocky and slopes downward, with a sharp arete and a big dihedral as the main features. Gear is thin on several routes, so many climbers set up a top rope. The walk from the road is short, and the crag draws very little traffic.

co_wigwam_dome.blurb: Wigwam Dome is a sunny, south-facing granite dome in the Lost Creek Wilderness of the South Platte region, at about 9,300 feet. It is the first dome you meet when hiking up the Wigwam Creek trail. All fifteen routes are traditional, mixing crack and slab climbing on coarse, large-crystal rock, and several run to multiple pitches, some up to seven. Grades spread from 5.8 to 5.12, with the bulk between 5.9 and 5.11. Expect a real day out in a wilderness setting, best suited to confident traditional leaders who like long, moderate lines.

co_2_canyon_amphitheater.blurb: Canyon Amphitheater is the first area you reach on the Pooka buttress in Staunton State Park, at the east end of Staunton Rocks. A slab with a steeper, cracked band above it sits beside a small canyon, and the wall gets morning sun with shade by late afternoon. The fifteen routes are nine sport, three trad and three top-rope lines, from very easy 5.4 slab climbing up through a solid group of 5.9s to a few 5.11 and 5.12 pitches. Some routes have two pitches. The area is fairly new, so expect the occasional loose block. Its easy options make it friendly for newer climbers.

co_06_surreal_estate.blurb: Surreal Estate is a sport wall on the north side of The Bank at Shelf Road, north of Canon City, at roughly 6,960 feet. It is one of two clean tan faces in the middle of the canyon, and the walk from the parking area is only a few minutes along the dirt road. All fifteen routes are bolted. The grades run from 5.9 to 5.13, but most sit between 5.11 and 5.12, so it rewards climbers who are comfortable on steady, sustained faces. It sits in one of the busiest parts of the Shelf Road scene, with a few 5.10 options as well.

co_a_east_wall.blurb: East Wall is the first face of the Lower Tier in the Tiers of Zion, above Clear Creek Canyon near Golden. It is a small, shorter slab, and most of its fifteen routes are single pitches of about 40 to 60 feet, with a few two- and three-pitch lines. It is a mix of gear and bolted routes. Grades lean easy to moderate, with many climbs between 5.4 and 5.8 and a handful of 5.10s, which makes it a good spot for newer leaders. The gneiss here is cool and shaded by trees, and direct sun arrives only in the afternoon. A narrow ledge runs below the wall and drops steeply, so keep small children away from the edge.
